"Amiss" means in a wrong, faulty, or unsatisfactory way — in a way that is not how it should be, not as expected, or not as it was supposed to turn out.

Think of it this way: imagine you have a plan, a process, or a situation, and instead of going the right way, it goes the wrong way, or something inside it is off, out of place, or broken. That's precisely where "amiss" lives.

The most common way you'll encounter "amiss" is in the phrase go amiss, which simply means to go wrong or to turn out badly.

  • "The experiment went amiss." → The experiment went wrong.
  • "Something went amiss during the surgery." → Something went wrong during the surgery.
  • "Everything went amiss that evening." → Everything that evening turned out badly.
  • "Nothing went amiss." → Everything went fine; nothing went wrong.

Notice how "nothing went amiss" flips the meaning neatly — if nothing went amiss, it means everything went as it should.
The Subtle Nuance: "Something Off," Not Always a Disaster

This is important. "Amiss" doesn't always mean something went spectacularly or obviously wrong. Very often, it describes a quiet, nagging sense that something is simply "off" — not quite right, not as expected — even when you can't immediately name or explain what the problem is.

For example:

  • "She walked into the room and immediately felt something was amiss."

There's no explosion, no obvious crisis. But something is wrong. Maybe a drawer is open that wasn't before. Maybe someone is avoiding her eyes. The word "amiss" captures that unsettling, subtle feeling perfectly.

This is why "amiss" is so often used in mystery, suspense, or situations where a problem is sensed before it is understood.
A Very Important Idiomatic Use: "Wouldn't Go Amiss"

This is one of the most useful — and slightly surprising — phrases built around "amiss." When you say something wouldn't go amiss, you mean that thing would be welcome, useful, or appreciated right now. It's a polite, understated way of saying you want or need something.

  • "A cup of tea wouldn't go amiss right now." → A cup of tea would be very welcome right now.
  • "A little extra help wouldn't go amiss." → Some extra help would be appreciated.
  • "An apology wouldn't go amiss." → An apology would be the right and fitting thing here.
  • "A good night's sleep wouldn't go amiss." → I really could do with a good night's sleep.

Why does this work? Because the speaker is saying the thing would not be wrong or out of place — which is a gentle understatement for "it would actually be quite right and very welcome." It's a soft, indirect, and often slightly humorous way of expressing a desire or a need.

To take something amiss means to feel offended, hurt, or slighted by something someone said or did — especially when that person perhaps didn't mean any harm. You're interpreting something in a negative light.

  • "Please don't take this amiss, but your report needs more work." → Please don't be offended by what I'm about to say.
  • "She took his playful teasing amiss." → She was hurt or upset by his teasing, even though he was just joking.
  • "I hope you won't take it amiss if I offer a suggestion." → I hope my suggestion won't offend you.

In practice, "take this amiss" is very commonly used as a polite cushion before saying something that might be sensitive or critical — a way of warning the listener not to be offended before you've even said the thing.
A Note on "Amiss" After Linking Verbs (Predicative Use)

You will very frequently see "amiss" placed after linking verbs like be, seem, feel, appear, and look. In these cases, it works more like an adjective describing the subject, but the meaning is the same — wrong, off, not right.

  • "Something is amiss." → Something is wrong.
  • "Nothing seems amiss." → Nothing appears to be wrong.
  • "Everything looked amiss." → Everything appeared to be in a wrong or broken state.

This is one of the special features of "amiss" — it almost always appears after the verb, never before a noun. You would never say "an amiss plan" or "the amiss situation." It's always positioned after: something went amiss, something is amiss, take it amiss. Keep this in mind and you'll always use it correctly.

Here is a short summary of everything "amiss" does, so you have it clearly in one place:

Core meaning — in a wrong, faulty, or unsatisfactory way; not as it should be.

"Go amiss" — to go wrong, to fail, to not turn out as expected.

"Wouldn't go amiss" — would be welcome, useful, or appreciated (a polite understatement).

"Take something amiss" — to feel offended or hurt by something, especially unintentionally.

The nuance — "amiss" often captures a subtle sense of something being off or out of place, not always a loud or obvious failure.

Grammatically — always appears after the verb or as part of a phrase, never directly in front of a noun.

Once you see all of this together, the word becomes very natural. When something isn't right — when a plan fails, when you sense trouble in a quiet room, when someone needs gentle reassurance before hearing a criticism, or when a cup of tea would honestly be just lovely — "amiss" is the word working quietly in the background.
